generated.title: A MASSIVE EARTHQUAKE IN NYC?! Myth or Fact? #shorts
generated.description:
Could a powerful earthquake really hit New York City? Myth or fact?

New York has been shaken before. On August 10, 1884, an earthquake estimated at magnitude 5.2 struck near New York City, probably somewhere between Brooklyn and Sandy Hook, New Jersey. Its magnitude is an estimate from historical damage reports, not an instrument reading. It damaged chimneys and brick buildings in New York and New Jersey and was felt from Virginia to Maine.

On April 5, 2024, a magnitude 4.8 earthquake, measured by USGS, struck Tewksbury Township, New Jersey, about 65 km west of New York City. Millions felt it, and the USGS received more than 180,000 "Did You Feel It?" reports, the most for any earthquake.

New York City's hazard mitigation plan cites the 2023 USGS hazard maps: a 5 to 25 percent chance of potentially damaging shaking (intensity VI or stronger) in the New York City area over 100 years. That is a long-term hazard estimate, not a prediction of any specific earthquake.

The main concern is not the skyscrapers. NYC Emergency Management counts more than 100,000 unreinforced brick buildings, most built between the mid-1800s and the 1930s, and most of the city's buildings predate its 1995 seismic code. Soft soils can amplify shaking, and aging underground infrastructure is vulnerable.

So could a damaging earthquake hit New York? Yes. Is a catastrophic one likely? No.

This educational video includes AI-generated illustrations: a fictional earthquake-disaster scene of a hypothetical scenario, a dramatized AI reconstruction of an 1884 street (not an archival photograph), and illustrative city views. They are not real footage or predictions.
